content_voiceover: This slide maps out how somatic mutations distribute across PNH, aplastic anemia, and MDS, and it's really testing whether you understand the overlap syndrome. Comparing aplastic anemia to MDS, aplastic anemia patients frequently carry BCOR or BCORL1 mutations, which are relatively specific to the immune-mediated marrow failure setting, and PNH clones driven by PIGA mutations are found in twenty to thirty percent of aplastic anemia patients and post-aplastic anemia MDS, but are rare, only about two percent, in primary hypocellular MDS. That distinction is a great board discriminator: a sizable PNH clone points you toward aplastic anemia or PNH itself rather than primary MDS. When you compare secondary MDS arising after aplastic anemia to primary hypocellular MDS, RUNX1, SETBP1, ASXL1, and deletion seven or seven q are more prevalent in post-aplastic anemia secondary MDS, while classic spliceosomal mutations, SF3B1, SRSF2, ZRSR2, and U2AF1, are relatively absent in secondary MDS compared to primary MDS. So the overall teaching point is that clonal evolution after immunosuppressive therapy for aplastic anemia follows a different mutational route than de novo MDS, favoring BCOR, RUNX1, and monosomy seven rather than the spliceosomal pathway.
keypoints: PNH clones: 20-30% in AA/post-AA-MDS vs only ~2% in primary hypo-MDS
BCOR/BCORL1 mutations frequent in AA, less so in de novo MDS
Post-AA secondary MDS: ↑RUNX1, SETBP1, ASXL1, del(7)/7q
Secondary MDS relatively lacks spliceosomal mutations (SF3B1, SRSF2, ZRSR2, U2AF1)
keypoint_voiceover: A large PNH clone, twenty to thirty percent, favors aplastic anemia or post-aplastic anemia MDS, while primary hypocellular MDS rarely shows a PNH clone. BCOR and BCORL1 mutations are enriched in aplastic anemia. When aplastic anemia evolves into secondary MDS, expect RUNX1, SETBP1, ASXL1, and deletion seven or seven q, but notably an absence of the spliceosomal mutations typical of primary MDS, like SF3B1 and SRSF2.
